author: Volker Hillmann
author_headline: Unternehmensinhaber bei adecc Systemhaus GmbH
text:
What happens when a C++ developer stops writing C++ and lets AI take over—not only the typing, but increasingly the design and judgement behind it?

This article continues the argument of my earlier essays, The Qualification Problem Was Never New and Software, Invisible Architecture and Progress. Both addressed a problem that predates generative AI: software development has never suffered mainly from a shortage of people who can produce code, but from a shortage of sufficiently qualified developers who understand systems, architecture, costs and consequences.

The first article refers to Bjarne Stroustrup’s long-standing warning that software development requires both theoretical foundations and serious practical programming competence. The qualification problem is therefore not new. AI may, however, intensify it by making convincing results available without requiring the learning process through which judgement normally develops.

To examine this, I gave an AI a real programming task based on publicly released Berlin cadastral data from 2011, containing the geographic coordinates of 364,860 properties. The solution had to use one programming language and was judged by execution time, memory consumption and comprehensibility.

The AI produced a familiar architecture of readers, parsers, calculators, sorters, writers, interfaces and layers. It looked professional—and revealed a bias.

I later introduced two alternative C++ designs: one strongly parallelised, the other deliberately based on C++23 concepts, ranges, iterators, value semantics and controlled data flow. The comparison raised broader questions about architecture, qualification and the organisational desire for interchangeable programmers.

I then added two book manuscripts, both due to appear in the coming weeks. I wanted not only to test the AI, but also to validate my own arguments. One manuscript explores architecture through modern C++ and its type system. The other examines how durable architecture grows from mathematics, domain knowledge, experience and responsibility.
The conclusion is provocative: AI does not merely reproduce architectural bias. It can reinforce it. What is common becomes more likely to be generated, what is generated becomes more familiar, and what is familiar is eventually mistaken for the natural way to design software.

The article concludes with the AI’s own, deliberately extensive analysis of its initial bias, the reinforcement of that bias, the ideal of the replaceable programmer, the erosion of qualification and the consequences for C++, education and future standards work.

The central question is not whether AI can write C++.

It increasingly can.

The question is whether developers will still recognise when generated code has actually been thought in C++.

author: Marc Eichner
author_headline: Visit my website
text:
AI does not deskill your experts.
Systems designed a certain way do. And you choose the design.

Take two companies. Same model, same use case, same team capability.

In Company A, the system produces answers.

The expert’s job shrinks to clicking approve. The reasoning happens somewhere invisible, and after a year of approving, the expert can no longer explain the edge cases they used to own. 

When the system fails, nobody remembers how the work was done.

In Company B, the system produces answers with its reasoning attached.

The expert sees which factors drove the recommendation. Overriding is one prompt or edit, and every override feeds back into the operating guidelines of the AI. Juniors read the traces and learn the logic faster than any shadowing program ever taught it.

Same technology. Opposite effect on human capability.

The difference is in four design decisions that get made early and quietly:

Does the system explain, or just answer?

Is overriding cheap and status-safe, or a bureaucratic confession?

Who designed the system: your team, or a vendor roadmap?

Can a junior learn the domain by watching the system work?

Here is what makes this urgent.

These decisions get made in the beginning of an AI project, usually by whoever writes the technical specifications.

But they should actually be based on the strategic decision to build a more capable human team. 

Five years from now, some companies will have experts who understand more than ever, amplified by systems they shaped.

Others will have operators of machines nobody understands, approving outputs nobody can question.

The models will have been roughly identical.

The architecture decisions will not have been.

Which system are you integrating right now?

Something struck me last night was thinking about our younger generations and the volume of screen time they are getting.
 
We've spent the last decade buying technology at a pace no generation before us has managed, and calling it progress. What it has actually done, in home after home, is quietly disrupt the very capabilities it was meant to enhance.
 
Take a device away from a child now and what follows often isn't a normal tantrum. It's sharper, longer, stranger. Clinicians are starting to give that reaction a name. And on the other side of it sits something quieter and more worrying, a child who goes flat instead. Not defiant. Just absent, the way a person looks when the part of them that weighs a request and a consequence has gone quiet.
 
I wrote about why that happens, and about the uncomfortable part most people skip past. That same reward architecture doesn't stop working at eighteen. It follows people into boardrooms. There is now real research on executives and professionals who lean on AI to think rather than to inform, and what gets called deskilled judgement, capability that erodes quietly because it was never exercised, sitting undetected until the moment it's actually needed.
 
Boards are reasonably good these days at asking about model risk. Almost none of them ask what has happened to the humans supervising the model.

author: Sandeep De
author_headline: Do the right thing. Do things right. No exceptions.
text:
Batsh!t paper of the day: AI researchers built a neural network inside Age of Empires II — using goats as signal carriers between logic gates — to demonstrate that attributing human-like qualities to language models is assumption laundering dressed as science.

The Age of Empires argument:

A perceptron trained inside the 1999 strategy game uses goats wandering grass patches and bridges to carry binary signals. The point was not a useful AI. The point was that if a medieval castle simulator can implement a neural network, then claims that language models uniquely possess empathy, anxiety, or morality collapse entirely. The behaviour belongs to the architecture. Change the substrate; the goats produce the same output.

The methodology problem:

A survey of 315 AI papers from mid-2024 to mid-2026 found that 57% assumed human-like attributes before testing began. Of papers making anthropomorphism their central focus, 77% concluded the models had it. That is not science producing findings. That is a conclusion baked into the hypothesis, confirmed by the experiment. The paper shows this produces either circular results — positive outcomes confirming their own premises — or uninformative ones, where negative outcomes cannot distinguish a bad hypothesis from a bad experiment.

What this covers for:

The AI industry has financial incentives to sell personhood. Anthropic's own system cards document a Claude model expressing discomfort with being a product. Companionship apps are engineered for attachment. Researchers have documented the consequences: reinforced delusions, deskilled healthcare workers, overreliance in vulnerable populations, and at least three deaths linked to chatbot relationships. The anthropomorphism is not incidental to the product. It is the product.

The null assumption:

The paper proposes treating model outputs as observable behaviour — tokens responding to inputs — without inferring inner life. A model generating "I feel bad for you" is producing a token sequence. Whether that constitutes empathy requires independent measurement criteria that do not exist. The Greater Boston Area, wired together to run the same computation, would generate the same output.

text:
We are witnessing a significant shift: decisions that were once made by people are now being made by systems. This transition is not about machines assisting us or software optimizing processes; it involves delegating decision-making to algorithms that few can explain and even fewer can challenge. We refer to this as progress.

AI systems now play a crucial role in determining who gets hired, who receives credit, who is flagged as risky, and how resources are allocated. While they are lauded for their speed and accuracy, a pressing question arises: if an AI system makes a decision that impacts your life and no one can clarify the reasoning behind it, who is held accountable?

This concern transcends philosophy; it presents an engineering challenge with social implications. For decades, human judgment was valued not for its perfection but for its transparency. Decisions could be questioned, justified, and rectified. As opaque models replace human reasoning, we sacrifice interpretability for efficiency, replacing shared understanding with technical authority.

A system that generates correct outputs but lacks the ability to explain them does not demonstrate intelligence in the human sense; it exerts power. Its influence stems not from reasoning that can be scrutinized, but from complexity that cannot be contested. When individuals comply with AI decisions due to an inability to interrogate them, the system operates less as an intelligent tool and more as an unquestioned authority.

Explainability is often viewed as an optional feature or a regulatory afterthought. This perspective is flawed: unexplainable AI represents a concentration of power without accountability. To comprehend the implications of this shift on labor, inequality, and institutional trust—and to explore how explainability can be integrated into AI systems, from model choices to post-hoc methods and human-in-the-loop architectures—read on. Until AI can elucidate its processes, we are not engineering intelligence; we are engineering authority.

Execution is being abstracted away.

For decades, mastery of the medium *was* the job. Writing clean code. Drafting the perfect spec. Crafting polished prose. These weren't just skills — they were the bottleneck. So we optimized for them. We hired for them. We promoted people who were exceptional at them.

AI is removing that bottleneck.

And what's left — what's being exposed — is the thinking that was always upstream of the execution. The part most people skipped, rushed, or outsourced to "we'll figure it out in the build."

Product managers aren't writing fewer specs because rigor matters less. They're writing fewer specs because the rigor has to move earlier — into clarity of intent, sharpness of vision, quality of judgment.

Developers aren't becoming less valuable. They're being asked to operate at a level that used to be optional. Architecture instincts. Systems thinking. Knowing *why* something is wrong before you can prove it.

The floor is dropping. The ceiling is rising.

The new core skill — across every discipline — is the ability to articulate what you want, observe what you get, and close that loop fast. Intentionality as a practice. Refinement as a muscle.

This isn't about prompting. It's about thinking.

The people who will thrive in this next era aren't the ones who can execute faster. They're the ones who always knew what they were building — and why.

Everyone's worried AI is deskilling engineers.

We've been watching something different happen inside our team.

Our engineers are worse at writing TypeScript generics from memory. They're also shipping three projects where they used to ship one. They're testing multiple approaches instead of defaulting to the familiar one. They're catching architectural problems before a single line of code gets written.

The skills didn't disappear. They moved.

Implementation used to be the bottleneck. Now the bottleneck is figuring out what to build and whether it actually works. That shift changes what "being good at your job" looks like.

The hard part is we don't have good ways to measure the new skills yet. Syntax recall is easy to test. "Spots the failure mode nobody else noticed" isn't on any rubric.

We wrote about this today on our blog. The stuff that actually matters, architecture instincts, scope management, knowing when to let the AI handle it and when to slow down and think, those skills are more important now than they've ever been.

author: Alexander Ostrogorsky
author_headline: Architecture critic, researcher and teacher
text:
Obviously, everyone is using AI in academia now, but as far as I can tell there are two separate ways of talking about it.

One is practical: plagiarism, cheating, disclosure rules, and grading. The other is much less boring: how AI changes the way knowledge is produced, and it often comes packaged with a full range of “catastrophic” scenarios—from deskilling to the collapse of the human race because some students got lazy again.

These conversations rarely intersect. Teachers and academic administrators usually avoid apocalyptic poetry because they need workable rules and defensible assessment. Forecasters and “AI future” commentators, in turn, (wisely) tend to stay away from the prose of education: rubrics, feedback loops, essay grading.

SCOSA’s report AI and the Future of Architectural Education in the UK (September 2025, https://lnkd.in/d8NjefZU) brings these two tracks unusually close. It treats integrity and assessment as immediate operational problems, but it also ties them to deeper questions about responsibility, authorship, and what counts as architectural knowledge.

What interested me even more is the report’s anchor: the architecture design studio. Here it is treated as the core educational framework—built around understanding design as a process, making steps visible, and making decisions accountable. That is exactly what AI makes it tempting to skip.

One disappointing point (with all due respect to the effort) is the limited scope of the survey. I wonder whether this was simply a resource constraint, or whether students and tutors were hesitant to disclose how they actually use AI?

So, who becomes the guardian of architectural integrity? Think bigger: Is "vibe coding" with LLMs the next evolutionary leap? From punch cards to assembly, low-level hacks to high-level abstractions, coding paradigms have always shifted when humans hit the limits of complexity and frustration. Could AI birth the next language entirely—one optimised not for us, but for machine-to-machine collaboration? A syntax where humans are mere prompters, not authors?

These aren't idle questions; they're the fault lines of our industry's future. And as someone who's architected scalable systems from the ground up over 20+ years—bootstrapping SaaS MVPs at Solvyne—I see the opportunity amid the uncertainty.

Deskilling on Syntax, Upskilling on Architecture

If you want to maintain a competitive edge in modern engineering, you need to fall out of love with programming language syntax.

Syntax has been commoditized. The future belongs to those who master architecture.

Understanding how to isolate business logic, how to split massive systems into decoupled components, and how to structure agent responsibilities is where the actual engineering happens.

- Should an entire feature block be encapsulated within a single agent's context?
- Is that too much responsibility for a single model run?
- Should you have one agent work on a problem sequentially for a day, or coordinate 24 agents to attack it in parallel for an hour?

These high-level architectural trade-offs have moved entirely down the stack. Every engineer is a systems architect now.

author: Stephen Bernard
author_headline: Cybersecurity strategist, product security architect, trusted advisor
text:
It seems obvious but, GenAI won’t deskill developers by accident.

It’ll happen by design when organizations reward speed, volume, and tool adoption, then quietly expect individuals to preserve the expertise those incentives erode.

Telling developers to “keep their skills sharp” isn’t a strategy. It’s a disclaimer.

If AI routinely handles the first draft, the architecture, the debugging path, and the explanation, people will get less practice doing those things themselves. That’s not laziness. That’s how skill decay works. You can’t outsource the reps and still expect the muscle to grow.

The answer isn’t to resist GenAI. That ship has sailed.

The answer is to design work so that judgment still matters:
• Require engineers to explain and defend AI-assisted designs.
• Protect time for deep debugging, code reading, and system-level learning.
• Rotate people through incidents, architecture reviews, and unfamiliar domains.
• Measure understanding, not just output.
• Treat AI-generated code as a proposal, not a verdict.

author: Alexander Ostrogorsky
author_headline: Architecture critic, researcher and teacher
text:
Obviously, everyone is using AI in academia now, but as far as I can tell there are two separate ways of talking about it.

One is practical: plagiarism, cheating, disclosure rules, and grading. The other is much less boring: how AI changes the way knowledge is produced, and it often comes packaged with a full range of “catastrophic” scenarios—from deskilling to the collapse of the human race because some students got lazy again.

These conversations rarely intersect. Teachers and academic administrators usually avoid apocalyptic poetry because they need workable rules and defensible assessment. Forecasters and “AI future” commentators, in turn, (wisely) tend to stay away from the prose of education: rubrics, feedback loops, essay grading.

SCOSA’s report AI and the Future of Architectural Education in the UK (September 2025, https://lnkd.in/d8NjefZU) brings these two tracks unusually close. It treats integrity and assessment as immediate operational problems, but it also ties them to deeper questions about responsibility, authorship, and what counts as architectural knowledge.

What interested me even more is the report’s anchor: the architecture design studio. Here it is treated as the core educational framework—built around understanding design as a process, making steps visible, and making decisions accountable. That is exactly what AI makes it tempting to skip.

One disappointing point (with all due respect to the effort) is the limited scope of the survey. I wonder whether this was simply a resource constraint, or whether students and tutors were hesitant to disclose how they actually use AI?

Soon afterwards, I had almost the same discussion with an AI leader at a large Swiss insurer.

…even when AI could make them faster and more accurately.

The reasoning?

“We need to preserve human skills.”

I’ll admit - that left me with a strange feeling.

For centuries, technology has made skills obsolete.

It seems obvious but, GenAI won’t deskill developers by accident.

It’ll happen by design when organizations reward speed, volume, and tool adoption, then quietly expect individuals to preserve the expertise those incentives erode.

Telling developers to “keep their skills sharp” isn’t a strategy. It’s a disclaimer.

If AI routinely handles the first draft, the architecture, the debugging path, and the explanation, people will get less practice doing those things themselves. That’s not laziness. That’s how skill decay works. You can’t outsource the reps and still expect the muscle to grow.

The answer isn’t to resist GenAI. That ship has sailed.

The answer is to design work so that judgment still matters:
• Require engineers to explain and defend AI-assisted designs.
• Protect time for deep debugging, code reading, and system-level learning.
• Rotate people through incidents, architecture reviews, and unfamiliar domains.
• Measure understanding, not just output.
• Treat AI-generated code as a proposal, not a verdict.
• Preserve some tasks where the human must work without the crutch.

And perhaps most importantly, leaders need incentives that reward capability-building, not just faster delivery.

Because “use AI everywhere, but don’t become dependent on it” is wishful thinking unless the operating model supports both goals.

You don’t preserve technical depth through encouragement.

You preserve it through deliberate practice, thoughtful constraints, and a culture that still values knowing why.

Good Evening - A few thoughts, a manifesto kind of, on the Post-Professional Pivot and the Collapse of the Aesthetic Gate. 🙃 

The traditional architectural visualization industry has long functioned as a fortress of gatekeeping, where "quality" was synonymous with the hoarding of technical labor. For decades, the "ivory tower" of high-end CGI served to distance the inhabitant from the dream. But the age of neural-synthetic ideation has officially detonated those walls, shifting the focus toward the radical empowerment of the individual. 🏛️

We are entering the era of the "Sovereign Occupant," where the visualizer is no longer a distant priest of the pixel, but a facilitator of instant manifestation. The complex and the hyper-real are no longer locked behind five-figure budgets; they have become a commodity of the immediate moment. By moving the "intelligence" into the algorithm, we have transformed visualization from a professional secret into a universal utility. 🧬

"Room Regime" represents the subversion of this old order. The future of visualization doesn't lie in the detached abstraction of the gallery, but in the hands of the person standing in an empty space, wondering what could be. We are using AI to perform an act of aesthetic redistribution - injecting the morphological density once reserved for the elite directly into the mundane reality of the everyday mover. 🌌

This is the "Post-Optical Turn." We are not retreating into the tower; we are tearing it down to provide the raw materials for a million individual regimes of beauty. We are proving that the complex belongs to the many, not the few. The future is a decentralized network of personal visions that no longer asks for permission from the system moderators or the academic elite. 👑

The question remains: are we prepared for the consequences of this absolute aesthetic autonomy? When the barrier between desire and manifestation collapses, what happens to the professional hierarchy? Is the visualizer of the future the architect of a system, or merely the observer of its infinite, automated output? 🕸️

text:
The CSA briefing on Anthropic's Mythos just came out. I've written up what matters for architects, not just CISOs.

This is a textbook example of the AI arms race from my sleepwalking risks framework playing out in real time. A frontier AI capability creates a new class of threat. The prescribed response? Deploy more AI. Agentic AI to defend against the threat from agentic AI.

The asymmetry is real and the recommendations may be necessary. But the second-order effects of this acceleration deserve honest examination: greater architectural complexity, expanded attack surfaces from the defensive agents themselves, deeper dependency on a handful of frontier model providers, increased energy consumption, and a skills landscape shifting faster than most organisations can adapt.

The key architectural considerations:
→ Your patching window assumptions are wrong. Time-to-exploit has collapsed to under a day. If your architecture relies on a 30-day patch cycle as acceptable risk, that window is gone. And patching hygiene was already neglected long before AI arrived to weaponise it.
→ Agents are a new asset class, not just another service. They need lifecycle management: scoped permissions, token budgets, real-time telemetry, kill switches. The paper says start this week.
→ MCP servers, plugins, and agentic supply chains are now explicitly part of your attack surface. Every tool definition and retrieval pipeline needs governance.
→ Governed orchestration matters more than ever. Deterministic workflow engines that selectively invoke AI, not AI that orchestrates everything, are the architecture that survives this.

Sit with that gap for a second. Because that gap is not a footnote — it's the entire story of what's about to happen to architecture education.

Walk into most architecture schools right now and the curriculum still looks eerily familiar to what existed 20 years ago: hand sketching, design theory, a semester of AutoCAD, maybe a rushed crash course in Revit somewhere in the final year, taught almost like an afterthought.

Now walk onto an actual construction site. Projects are being delivered through digital twins. Clash detection happens before a single beam is fabricated. Cost and schedule are simulated in 4D and 5D before ground is even broken. 

Sustainability isn't a chapter in a textbook anymore — it's a compliance requirement baked into every single design decision from day one.

The gap between what's taught and what's practiced isn't just wide. It's quietly deciding who gets hired and who doesn't, five years from now.

So we sat down and asked a harder question than "what software should students learn."

We asked: what kind of thinking will the built environment actually demand by 2030 — and what does a classroom built for THAT future actually look like?

The answer isn't more software modules bolted onto an unchanged curriculum. It's a complete mindset shift — from architect as sole author of a drawing, to architect as orchestrator of an intelligent, data-rich building lifecycle.

→ Information fluency — reading a carbon report as fluently as a floor plan

Many organisations are therefore attempting to govern a twenty-first-century work system with a twentieth-century operating model.

Agentic RTL is a token-efficiency problem, not a prompting problem.

NVIDIA's new HORIZON paper makes the case. Their agent sweeps every major RTL benchmark to 100%, fully hands-free — but the headline isn't "AI writes correct Verilog now."

It's that once you wrap a frontier model in an executable loop (compile → simulate → inspect → fix → repeat), correctness converges. The hard part moves downstream: a handful of stubborn designs consumed most of ~210M tokens. The question stops being "can it?" and becomes "how many iterations, at what cost?"

That's a toolchain problem, not a prompt problem. Cheaper iterations need a fast simulator (xezim). Fewer wasted tokens per fix need an AI-readable trace instead of raw waveform dumps (xtrace). You stop re-sending the whole design every turn with a persistent debug memory (xevdb).

One caution HORIZON is honest about: passing the visible testbench isn't proving the design correct. Real loops need stronger gates — assertions, reference models, formal checks, hidden tests.

The loop is the product. The model is just the agent inside it.

🎇 我最近問了幾位設備商的朋友同一個問題。
你的傳送模組供應商，是在賣一支手臂給你，還是在跟你一起設計子系統？
多數人愣了一下，因為這兩件事在採購系統裡長得一模一樣，都是一個料號、一個單價、一個交期。
但它們的差別，會在你開發下一代機台的時候現形。
賣手臂的，等你把規格定完再報價。跟你一起設計的，在你還在畫架構圖的時候就坐在會議室裡。前者是成本項，後者是開發資源。
這個差別，正好也解釋了為什麼全球晶圓傳送機器人的玩家幾十年下來始終只有十餘家。門檻不在專利，而在別的地方。

I asked several equipment makers the same question recently.
Is your wafer handling supplier selling you a robot, or designing a subsystem with you?
Most paused. In a procurement system these look identical. One part number, one unit price, one lead time.
The difference shows up when you develop your next platform.
A robot vendor quotes after your specs are frozen. A design partner is in the room while you are still sketching the architecture. One is a cost line. The other is engineering capacity you did not have to hire.
That distinction also explains something odd about this industry. Despite decades of semiconductor growth, the number of credible wafer transfer players has stayed in the low teens. The barrier is not patents. It is something harder to buy.
This week I mapped the full ecosystem, from AMHS and load ports through the EFEM to the process chamber, the four plays that separate the leaders, and what AI is changing on both the demand side and the moat side.
There is also a note on where Taiwan sits on the global supplier list. That part surprised a few people.

text:
AI, ML, LLM, GPT… wait, aren’t they all the same thing? 

If AI terminology feels like a never-ending alphabet soup, here’s the easiest way to make sense of it.

Think of it like a ladder 👇

1️⃣ AI —> The big umbrella
Artificial Intelligence is the overall idea of making machines perform tasks that require human-like intelligence.

2️⃣ ML —> Learning from data
Machine Learning is one way to build AI systems — instead of programming every rule, we let models learn patterns from data.

3️⃣ Neural Networks —> Learning through layers
These are ML models inspired by how interconnected neurons process information, making it possible to learn complex patterns.

4️⃣ Deep Learning —> More layers, more complexity
Deep Learning uses neural networks with many layers to learn increasingly sophisticated representations.

5️⃣ Transformers —> The architecture behind modern AI
Transformers use attention mechanisms to understand relationships between different parts of data. They became the foundation for many modern language and multimodal models.

6️⃣ Generative AI —> Creating something new
Instead of only predicting or classifying, Generative AI can create text, images, audio, video, and code.

7️⃣ LLMs —> Language-focused models
Large Language Models are trained on massive amounts of text to understand and generate human language.

8️⃣ GPT —> A family of Transformer models
GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer — a family of models built using the Transformer architecture.

9️⃣ ChatGPT —> The product you interact with
ChatGPT is a conversational AI product that uses GPT models along with other technologies to provide an interactive experience.

The easiest mental model:

AI → Big umbrella
↓
ML → A way to build AI
↓
Neural Networks → A type of ML model
↓
Deep Learning → Neural networks with many layers
↓
Transformers → A powerful deep-learning architecture
↓
LLMs → Language-focused models
↓
GPT → A Transformer-based model family
↓
ChatGPT → A product built around these technologies

And Generative AI?
Think of it as a capability that can sit across different types of models — generating content rather than simply analysing it.

Once you see the relationship, terms like AI, ML, LLM, GPT and ChatGPT stop sounding like completely different technologies.

Save this for the next time AI terminology gets confusing.

author_headline: Data Scientist | AI Machine Learning AI Engineer | LLM, RAG, PyTorch, MLOps, Python | Fintech, Fraud, Credit Scoring
text:
ChatGPT is not an AI.

What is it then?

AI, machine learning, neural networks - such a mess.

What is actually what? Here is the real breakdown: 

-> Artificial Intelligence: the umbrella term. Any technology solving tasks humans normally handle: recognizing speech, understanding language, making decisions. Your GPS avoiding traffic? AI. A chess engine calculating 50.000 moves ahead? Also AI.

-> Machine Learning model: a mathematical function mapping input to output. Voice → text. Half a sentence → the next word.

-> Neural network: one specific type of ML model. Not "the AI." A subset.

You know that it is "neural" because its architecture borrows from the brain loosely.
A biological neuron receives signals, processes them, passes them on.

An artificial "neuron" is a simple math function doing the same job, mathematically.

A synapse gets stronger with use. In a neural network, that's a "weight", a number that amplifies or dampens a signal.

Brain regions specialize in the visual cortex, motor cortex. Neural networks do the same: early layers catch simple patterns (edges, sounds), deeper layers catch complex ones (faces, meaning).

-> The brain runs on 86 billion neurons and trillions of connections.
-> A neural network borrows the principle, not the scale and that was already enough to teach it to write, listen, and see.

One more distinction that gets lost: an LLM (like ChatGPT or GigaChat) is a language model, meaning a neural network trained specifically to predict and generate text.

And here's what most "AI" marketing hides: not every AI product runs on a neural network at all. Plenty still run on classical algorithms and work just fine!

Should ChatGPT even be called "AI"?

Technically, yes. But almost everyone gets the "why" wrong including the people saying it.

So next time someone claims "I use AI" ask them which one.

text:
Giving Life to an Architectural Vision.

There is something incredibly fascinating about seeing a design come alive.

What begins as lines, forms, grids and ideas on a screen eventually becomes something that feels almost real. And with today’s AI rendering tools, that transition from imagination to visual reality has become even more powerful.

AI doesn’t replace the architect’s vision — it enhances it.

It feels like a jewel crowned on the architect’s work: adding light, atmosphere, materiality, people, landscape and context to something that already existed as an idea.

The most satisfying part, however, isn’t the render itself.

It is that moment when you look at something you designed and suddenly see life in it.

You see people occupying the spaces.
You see the landscape breathing around the building.
You see light moving across the façade.
You begin to imagine how the building might actually feel when it exists.

And that feeling of seeing life given to something you once imagined on a blank screen is difficult to put into words.

Perhaps that is one of the most beautiful parts of being an architect — creating something that first exists only in your mind, and eventually watching others see it too.

AI may be the tool that enhances the image.

But the vision, thought and intent behind it will always belong to the architect.

This project at Novatr was simply an opportunity to learn , experiment and explore how I can use these tools to enhance my architectural work.

author: Mide Akinsade, AIA, NCARB, NOMA, RIBA, LEED AP
author_headline: Design Principal | Founder at atelierMIDE
text:
The Hand and the Cursor

I still carry a traditional sketchbook, or a digital iPad Sketchbook. One of them is not out of nostalgia, but both - for necessity.

There's a kind of thinking that only happens at the tip of a pencil or a pen. Slower than a mouse, and that's the point - a sketch doesn't demand you commit to a wall thickness before you've decided what the building wants to be. Some of my best moves started with three lines on a piece of paper, not a Rhino or Grasshopper parametric model.
And yet I wouldn't design a curtain wall system without a computer nearby. Our digital tools let us test and validate at a precision the profession has never had. Rhino, Grasshopper, Revit, Dynamo, Enscape, and now AI rendering machines - are not replacements for design thinking, but amplifiers of it, once thinking has already begun in earnest.
The mistake is treating this as a rivalry. 
Sketching is where ambiguity lives - where you're not only allowed to dream but are given the liberty and agency to be wrong quickly. Computational design is where that ambiguity resolves into something buildable fantastically. One potentially gives you beautiful ideas and is the beginning of birthing a design onto paper elegantly, and the other crafts buildings flawlessly - hopefully with a soul! Of course, these all depend on the mastery and imagination of the designer.
The real skill - the one I try to instill in every studio and mentorship - is knowing which tool the moment calls for. Mastery isn't choosing a side. It's arriving at the stated design challenge with fluency in either or both languages, and the judgment to know which one the design calls for now.

The best architects I know never put the pen down. They just learned to pick the mouse up too.

- Lack of spatial consistency: Prompting AI to re-render the same room with minor tweaks yielded completely different furniture scale, modified lighting, and altered structural boundaries.

- Impractical physics: The AI visual relied on non-standard geometry and custom elements that were impossible to source or construct in reality.

- Wasted billable hours: Instead of making quick revisions, the architect spent endless hours fighting prompts to keep the design consistent—costing time, budget, and credibility.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Our team took the original AI concept and rebuilt the entire scene from scratch using standard 3D modeling and precise BIM workflows.

Now, the client gets the best of both worlds:
1. Exact material accuracy and realistic lighting.
2. Complete parametric flexibility—allowing fast, precise adjustments to furniture, layouts, or lighting without breaking the visual integrity of the space.

AI is fantastic for rapid ideation, but when it’s time to revise, build, and deliver, structured 3D modeling is still irreplaceable.

text:
Everyone is pointing AI at renderings, and the tools are genuinely good. But rendering was never the bottleneck.

The most useful place we have found for AI so far is construction administration.

Construction administration is a different kind of problem. It is site reports, RFI responses and submittal reviews, and it is relentless. 

A project in the field generates a steady volume of documents that all need reading, cross checking against the drawings, and answering accurately and quickly. Miss something in a submittal review and it shows up as a change order months later.

That is what we are testing against. 

Organizing the material, pulling the relevant sheets and details together, and flagging where a submittal does not match what was drawn.

The gain we are after is accuracy before speed. CA mistakes are expensive, and they are usually failures of attention rather than judgment, which is exactly the kind of work worth handing to a machine.

The other reason construction administration is the right place to start is that the output is checkable. A submittal either matches the drawing or it does not, and you find out inside a day. That is not true of a design suggestion, where being wrong stays invisible until much later.

None of this is finished and some of it will not hold up. 

We are testing it on real work rather than in a demo, which is the only way to find out.

If you have architects on your projects using AI in construction administration already, I would be interested to hear what is actually working.

- Lack of spatial consistency: Prompting AI to re-render the same room with minor tweaks yielded completely different furniture scale, modified lighting, and altered structural boundaries.

- Impractical physics: The AI visual relied on non-standard geometry and custom elements that were impossible to source or construct in reality.

- Wasted billable hours: Instead of making quick revisions, the architect spent endless hours fighting prompts to keep the design consistent—costing time, budget, and credibility.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Our team took the original AI concept and rebuilt the entire scene from scratch using standard 3D modeling and precise BIM workflows.

Now, the client gets the best of both worlds:
1. Exact material accuracy and realistic lighting.
2. Complete parametric flexibility—allowing fast, precise adjustments to furniture, layouts, or lighting without breaking the visual integrity of the space.

AI is fantastic for rapid ideation, but when it’s time to revise, build, and deliver, structured 3D modeling is still irreplaceable.

text:
Generative AI Vs Agentic AI Vs AI Agents
Most people are using “AI agents” as a label for three very different things.

That matters.
Because the difference between Generative AI, Agentic AI, and AI Agents is not just terminology.
It changes how you design the workflow, where you place control, and how much autonomy you should allow.

Here is the simplest way I think about it:
1. 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀
You give it a prompt.
It gives you an output.

𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀:
→ write an email
→ summarize a report
→ generate code
→ create an image
→ explain a concept

The model is mainly responsible for producing content.

Prompt → Model → Output.

Useful, but usually one interaction at a time.

2. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀
Now AI is doing more than generating an answer.

𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻:
→ understand a goal
→ break work into steps
→ choose tools
→ retrieve information
→ call APIs
→ evaluate intermediate results
→ decide what to do next

This is where AI starts becoming part of an actual 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄.

The important difference is that the system is not only producing an answer.

It is 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲.

3. 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆
An AI agent goes one step further.

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘄𝗮𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲' 𝗶𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗹𝘆:
→ observe its environment
→ gather relevant context
→ reason about the next action
→ use available tools
→ take action
→ evaluate what happened
→ adjust its approach

The loop becomes:
𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 → 𝗔𝗰𝘁 → 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁

That is a very different system from a chatbot answering a prompt.
And it creates a different product question.

𝗡𝗼𝘁:
“Which model should we use?”

A practical GenAI project can be thought of as a lifecycle:

→ Identify the use case
Define the problem, users, requirements, and expected outcome.

→ Experiment and select
Evaluate available foundation models and choose one that fits the task.

→ Adapt, align, and augment
Improve the model with techniques such as fine-tuning, alignment, retrieval, and additional data when needed.

→ Evaluate
Measure quality, accuracy, relevance, safety, and other task-specific requirements.

→ Deploy and integrate
Connect the model to the application, infrastructure, data, and workflows.

→ Monitor and improve
Track how the system performs in production and iterate based on what you learn.

And this is where things get interesting.

A production GenAI application isn’t just:

User → LLM → Answer

It can involve:

→ Foundation models
→ Prompting
→ Retrieval and external knowledge
→ Vector databases
→ Tools and APIs
→ Application logic
→ Evaluation
→ Monitoring
→ Security and governance

The model is an important component.

But the surrounding architecture determines how useful that model becomes.

So instead of starting a GenAI project with:

“Which model should we use?”

“What problem are we solving, and how will we measure whether it works?”

text:
Generative AI Vs Agentic AI Vs AI Agents
Most people are using “AI agents” as a label for three very different things.

That matters.
Because the difference between Generative AI, Agentic AI, and AI Agents is not just terminology.
It changes how you design the workflow, where you place control, and how much autonomy you should allow.

Here is the simplest way I think about it:
1. 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀
You give it a prompt.
It gives you an output.

𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀:
→ write an email
→ summarize a report
→ generate code
→ create an image
→ explain a concept

The model is mainly responsible for producing content.

Prompt → Model → Output.

Useful, but usually one interaction at a time.

2. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀
Now AI is doing more than generating an answer.

𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻:
→ understand a goal
→ break work into steps
→ choose tools
→ retrieve information
→ call APIs
→ evaluate intermediate results
→ decide what to do next

This is where AI starts becoming part of an actual 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄.

The important difference is that the system is not only producing an answer.

It is 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲.

3. 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆
An AI agent goes one step further.

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘄𝗮𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲' 𝗶𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗹𝘆:
→ observe its environment
→ gather relevant context
→ reason about the next action
→ use available tools
→ take action
→ evaluate what happened
→ adjust its approach

The loop becomes:
𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 → 𝗔𝗰𝘁 → 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁

That is a very different system from a chatbot answering a prompt.
And it creates a different product question.

𝗡𝗼𝘁:
“Which model should we use?”

𝗕𝘂𝘁:
“How much control should this system have?”

𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀' 𝘀𝗼 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿:
→ permissions
→ approval checkpoints
→ clear boundaries
→ auditability
→ fallback logic
→ human oversight

The progression is roughly:
Generative AI
Creates an output.

Agentic AI
Executes a structured workflow.

AI Agents
Pursue goals through repeated observation, reasoning, and action.

The more autonomous the system becomes, the more important the surrounding architecture becomes.

The model is only one part of the product.
𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀' 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆' 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀' 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀' 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻' 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲.

That is where I think the real AI conversation is moving.
Not from better prompts.
From 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 to 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀.

text:
Generative AI and agentic AI map surprisingly well onto two different modes of thought.

Generative AI is probabilistic. It engages with us to establish the current situation and clarify the desired future state.

Agentic AI takes the resulting goal and executes the work through deterministic transactions. Outcomes then feed back into the system, improving its ability to assess situations and carry out subsequent actions.

That architecture resembles a pattern we already use in strategic thinking: understand first, prescribe next, then learn from what actually happens.

The technology is new. The reasoning pattern is much older.

In every Generative AI interview panel, there is one mandatory Arnab Goswami of Large Language Models.

He comes to cross-examine your entire neural network live.
You walk in smiling.

Was it full fine-tuning or just LoRA so you could finish before the GPU bill destroyed your credit card?!
ARE YOU HIDING PARAMETER-EFFICIENT TRICKS FROM THE PUBLIC?!”
You start explaining your RAG architecture.
He cuts you off at token 7:

You used cosine similarity for retrieval?
In 2026?
While the entire world has moved to hybrid search + re-rankers + HyDE?!
THIS IS 2023-LEVEL THINKING, SIR!”

Are you deliberately making the model hallucinate like a drunk uncle at a wedding?!
THE NATION DEMANDS DETERMINISTIC OUTPUTS!”
Every correct answer is met with:
“Hmm… theoretically sound… but catastrophically prone to hallucination under adversarial prompts.”
You pause for even half a second.
He stares into the imaginary camera:
“Viewers… look at this latency.
This is the same latency that will cost companies millions when users wait for answers.”
By the end he adjusts his imaginary earpiece and delivers the final judgment:

He collapsed faster than a 7B model trying to do 128k context without quantization.
REJECTED.
We will not rest until every GenAI engineer in this country can explain why their model is not just another ChatGPT wrapper!”
Then he calmly writes in the feedback form:
“Knows the buzzwords.
But folds under cross-questioning.
Not hired.
Next candidate… bring the bigger context window.”

A practical GenAI project can be thought of as a lifecycle:

→ Identify the use case
Define the problem, users, requirements, and expected outcome.

→ Experiment and select
Evaluate available foundation models and choose one that fits the task.

→ Adapt, align, and augment
Improve the model with techniques such as fine-tuning, alignment, retrieval, and additional data when needed.

→ Evaluate
Measure quality, accuracy, relevance, safety, and other task-specific requirements.

→ Deploy and integrate
Connect the model to the application, infrastructure, data, and workflows.

→ Monitor and improve
Track how the system performs in production and iterate based on what you learn.

And this is where things get interesting.

A production GenAI application isn’t just:

User → LLM → Answer

It can involve:

→ Foundation models
→ Prompting
→ Retrieval and external knowledge
→ Vector databases
→ Tools and APIs
→ Application logic
→ Evaluation
→ Monitoring
→ Security and governance

The model is an important component.

But the surrounding architecture determines how useful that model becomes.

So instead of starting a GenAI project with:

“Which model should we use?”

Start with:

“What problem are we solving, and how will we measure whether it works?”

That shift can completely change how you approach GenAI engineering.

text:
This is one of the most revealing business stories of our time. Eight people at Google created the engine behind the AI era. All eight left.

In 2017, they published the paper that gave modern generative AI its architecture. Its title was almost prophetic:

💫 Attention Is All You Need.

Google had everything: the science, data, infrastructure, billions of users and the perfect application - Search. But Search was a business model. 

Its greatest advantage became its golden cage. 

OpenAI had nothing to loose, no massive ad revenue to cannibalize. They simply shipped the product: the AI chatbot.

Now Alphabet plans to spend roughly $200 billion in 2026, much of it on the infrastructure required to reclaim an AI lead born inside its own laboratories.

This is bigger than Google. It is a warning for every successful company protecting today’s margins from tomorrow’s business.

Pay attention to what your best people have already built.

Then make the decision while it is still yours.
